courses.title: Neurological Physiotherapy
courses.description: Neurological assessment and rehabilitation of stroke, spinal cord injury, traumatic brain injury, Parkinson's disease, peripheral neuropathies and cerebral palsy.

topics.title: Neurological Assessment and Recovery
topics.summary: Tone, motor control, balance assessment, neuroplasticity and treatment approaches.

material.heading: Assessment
material.body: Neurological assessment covers consciousness (Glasgow Coma Scale), cognition and communication, tone (spasticity graded by the Modified Ashworth Scale 0–4; spasticity is velocity-dependent resistance from upper motor neuron lesions, while rigidity is velocity-independent — lead-pipe or cogwheel in Parkinson's), power, sensation (light touch, proprioception), coordination (finger–nose, heel–shin; ataxia in cerebellar lesions), reflexes (brisk with Babinski sign in UMN lesions; reduced in LMN lesions), balance (Berg Balance Scale — score < 45 indicates fall risk), gait and functional mobility (Timed Up and Go, 10-metre walk test), and activities of daily living (Barthel Index, Functional Independence Measure).

material.heading: Neuroplasticity and approaches
material.body: Recovery after brain injury relies on neuroplasticity — the nervous system's ability to reorganise through synaptic strengthening and recruitment of other areas. Principles of experience-dependent plasticity: use it or lose it, specificity, repetition (high doses of practice), intensity, salience (meaningful tasks) and timing (early rehabilitation). Treatment approaches: task-oriented training (practising real functional tasks), motor relearning programme (Carr and Shepherd), constraint-induced movement therapy (restrain the unaffected arm to force use of the affected arm — for patients with some wrist and finger extension), Bobath/neurodevelopmental treatment (normalising movement patterns), proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation (PNF — diagonal patterns), mirror therapy, and functional electrical stimulation. Evidence favours high-intensity, repetitive, task-specific practice.
keyPoints: Neuroplasticity: use it or lose it

topics.title: Stroke Rehabilitation
topics.summary: Stroke presentation, early positioning, motor recovery, shoulder care and gait retraining.

material.heading: Early management
material.body: Stroke is a leading cause of adult disability in Nigeria, driven largely by uncontrolled hypertension; haemorrhagic strokes are relatively common. Patients present with hemiplegia, sensory loss, aphasia (dominant hemisphere), neglect (non-dominant, usually right hemisphere), dysphagia and visual field loss. Early rehabilitation in a stroke unit improves outcomes; physiotherapy starts once the patient is medically stable (usually within 24–48 hours, avoiding very early high-dose mobilisation). Positioning prevents contractures, pressure sores and shoulder injury: alternate side-lying, supported sitting, and avoiding pulling on the affected arm. Dysphagia screening precedes oral intake to prevent aspiration pneumonia. Brunnstrom described stages of motor recovery from flaccidity through synergy patterns to isolated movement.

material.heading: Recovery and complications
material.body: Most motor recovery occurs within the first 3–6 months, though improvement can continue for years. Hemiplegic shoulder pain is common — caused by subluxation (in the flaccid stage), spasticity, adhesive capsulitis or complex regional pain syndrome; prevented by proper positioning, arm supports and avoiding traction on the arm (never pull the patient up by the affected arm); electrical stimulation can reduce subluxation. Gait retraining addresses weight shift, stance control, foot clearance (ankle–foot orthosis for foot drop) and walking speed, often with treadmill training. Upper limb rehabilitation uses repetitive task practice, CIMT and mirror therapy. Complications also include falls, depression, spasticity (stretching, positioning, botulinum toxin) and deconditioning; aerobic training and secondary prevention education (blood pressure control, medication adherence) are essential.
keyPoints: Never pull on the affected arm

topics.title: Spinal Cord Injury
topics.summary: Classification, complications, functional outcomes and rehabilitation.

material.heading: Classification and acute care
material.body: Spinal cord injury (SCI) in Nigeria is commonly caused by road traffic accidents, falls (including from palm trees) and violence. The ASIA Impairment Scale classifies injuries: A (complete — no motor or sensory function in S4–S5), B (sensory incomplete), C and D (motor incomplete, with D having at least half of key muscles below the level ≥ grade 3) and E (normal). Tetraplegia results from cervical injuries; paraplegia from thoracic, lumbar or sacral injuries. Incomplete syndromes include central cord (arms weaker than legs, older people with hyperextension), Brown-Séquard (ipsilateral motor and proprioceptive loss, contralateral pain and temperature loss) and anterior cord syndrome. Acute care includes spinal precautions, respiratory care (cervical lesions above C5 impair the diaphragm — C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive), positioning and passive movements.

material.heading: Complications and rehabilitation
material.body: Complications: autonomic dysreflexia (lesions at or above T6 — a noxious stimulus below the lesion such as a full bladder triggers dangerous hypertension, headache and bradycardia; sit the patient up and remove the cause), pressure ulcers (turn every 2 hours, pressure-relieving cushions), orthostatic hypotension, DVT, urinary tract infections, spasticity, contractures, heterotopic ossification and osteoporosis. Rehabilitation aims for maximal independence according to level: C6 (tenodesis grip, manual wheelchair with adaptations), T1 and below (full upper limb function, independent wheelchair use), low thoracic–lumbar (possible walking with orthoses). Training includes transfers, wheelchair skills, pressure relief, respiratory care, strengthening and community reintegration. Vocational rehabilitation and accessible environments are major challenges in Nigeria.
keyPoints: Autonomic dysreflexia ≥ T6: sit up, remove cause

topics.title: Progressive and Peripheral Neurological Conditions
topics.summary: Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, Guillain–Barré syndrome, peripheral neuropathy and Bell's palsy.

material.heading: Parkinson's disease and MS
material.body: Parkinson's disease (dopamine loss in the substantia nigra) causes bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor and postural instability, with a shuffling festinating gait, freezing and falls. Physiotherapy uses external cues (visual lines on the floor, auditory metronome rhythms), large amplitude movement training (LSVT BIG), balance and strength training, and fall prevention; timing sessions when medication is 'on' helps. Multiple sclerosis (demyelination; relapsing–remitting commonly; less common in Africa) causes fatigue, weakness, spasticity, ataxia and sensory symptoms; rehabilitation includes energy conservation, aerobic and strengthening exercise (avoiding overheating — Uhthoff's phenomenon), balance training and aids.

material.heading: Peripheral conditions
material.body: Guillain–Barré syndrome is an acute inflammatory polyneuropathy (often after infection) causing ascending symmetrical flaccid weakness and areflexia; it may involve respiratory muscles (monitor vital capacity; ventilation if needed). Physiotherapy: respiratory care, positioning, passive movements in the acute phase, then gradual strengthening avoiding over-fatigue; most recover. Peripheral neuropathy (diabetes, HIV, leprosy, alcohol) causes glove-and-stocking sensory loss, weakness and balance problems — foot care and balance training are key. Bell's palsy is idiopathic facial (VII) nerve palsy with lower motor neuron facial weakness (including the forehead); eye protection, steroids and facial exercises help, and most recover within months. Nerve injuries (e.g. radial nerve palsy — wrist drop; common peroneal — foot drop) need splinting and re-education.
keyPoints: Radial: wrist drop; peroneal: foot drop

topics.title: Paediatric Neurology and Brain Injury
topics.summary: Cerebral palsy, spina bifida, traumatic brain injury and developmental assessment.

material.heading: Cerebral palsy and spina bifida
material.body: Cerebral palsy (CP) is a group of permanent, non-progressive disorders of movement and posture due to disturbances in the developing brain; common Nigerian causes include birth asphyxia, neonatal jaundice (kernicterus) and infections such as meningitis. Types: spastic (most common — hemiplegic, diplegic, quadriplegic), dyskinetic (athetoid, often after kernicterus) and ataxic. The Gross Motor Function Classification System (GMFCS levels I–V) grades mobility. Management: family-centred therapy, positioning, stretching, strengthening, orthoses, mobility aids, goal-directed functional training and caregiver education; botulinum toxin and orthopaedic surgery for contractures. Spina bifida (neural tube defect, preventable with folic acid) — myelomeningocele causes lower limb paralysis, sensory loss, hydrocephalus and bladder problems; rehabilitation focuses on mobility, skin care and orthoses.
keyPoints: Folic acid prevents neural tube defects

material.heading: Traumatic brain injury
material.body: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is common after road traffic crashes, especially involving motorcycles (okada) without helmets. Severity by Glasgow Coma Scale: mild 13–15, moderate 9–12, severe ≤ 8. Acute physiotherapy in intensive care addresses respiratory care (with attention to intracranial pressure — avoid head-down positions and excessive coughing stimulation), positioning, and preventing contractures. Rehabilitation manages motor deficits, balance, cognitive and behavioural problems (agitation, memory, impulsivity) using structured, consistent routines and multidisciplinary input. The Rancho Los Amigos scale describes cognitive recovery stages. Prevention (helmets, seat belts, road safety) is the most effective strategy.
keyPoints: Avoid raising ICP in acute care
